fields.description: Five questions covering the same topics on every attempt. Pass with at least three correct.

fields.title: Follow the Pacific Connection
fields.content:
The Manila-Acapulco galleon trade connected the Philippines and Mexico across the Pacific Ocean. Acapulco was a port in New Spain, in what is now Mexico. The trade is commonly dated 1565-1815. These dates describe this trading connection, not the beginning or end of all Philippine trade. Earlier lessons already showed people exchanging goods before Spanish rule.

Our route diagram connects named places with arrows. It is a relationship guide, not a navigation chart: real voyages did not follow a straight line across a small page. Wind, currents and the direction of travel mattered. Trace Manila to Acapulco, then trace the connection back. A line can show a link between ports without telling us the time, cargo or outcome of every crossing. To investigate a particular voyage, look for its own dated records.

fields.title: Goods and Silver Moved Through a Network
fields.content:
Asian goods such as silk and porcelain traveled through Manila toward Acapulco. Silver moved from the Americas toward Manila, helping pay for goods. Manila was a meeting point within a wider network: goods leaving its port were not necessarily all made in the Philippines. Ask where an item was produced as well as which port shipped it.

Try a fictional cargo-card sort. A card says porcelain was loaded in Manila, but does not name its maker. Another card identifies an item as made in China. The loading port and production place answer different questions. Our symbols stand for examples, not the complete contents of a particular ship. A cargo list also cannot prove that every item arrived, that every voyage carried the same mixture, or that all people shared the proceeds. Compare departure and arrival records when the question concerns delivery.

fields.title: Look Beyond the Cargo
fields.content:
A ship and its cargo depended on people. Makers produced goods, workers prepared supplies, crews handled voyages, and traders arranged exchange. Obispados study of the sixteenth-century trade discusses household production, weaving and work related to moving cargo. Seeing a valuable object should lead us to ask about the work behind it, not only its selling price.

Our fictional task cards identify making cloth, preparing a ship and recording cargo. These are different roles in a connected system. One person could perform more than one role, and the work should not be described as identical for every place and period. An account naming a merchant may leave other workers unnamed. Do not conclude that unnamed people did no work. Earlier lessons also showed that colonial labor demands could be compulsory; a cargo value alone tells us neither consent nor fair payment.

fields.title: A Departure Was Not an Arrival
fields.content:
A long sea crossing involved uncertainty. Weather, ship condition, supplies and other dangers could affect a voyage. A departure entry records a ship leaving; it does not guarantee arrival or show the whole journey. The National Archives account of the Nuestra Senora de Covadonga illustrates how a particular ships papers can open questions about cargo and a voyage affected by capture.

We do not reenact an attack or award points for harm. Instead, use a fictional source desk: a departure note, a cargo list and a later arrival entry. Check that they concern the same vessel and journey before connecting them. A successful arrival does not prove that every crossing was safe; a loss does not prove every voyage failed. The teaching ship is a symbol, not a reconstruction of that named vessel. Your task is to explain what each record supports and what remains unknown.

fields.title: Connections Did Not Mean Equal Benefits
fields.content:
The trading connection moved objects, money and ideas across places. The Metropolitan Museum discusses how Asian goods could influence art in the Americas. A connection can change what people make and use. But the presence of valuable cargo is not proof that every person or community became wealthy. Benefits, costs and choices need evidence about the people involved.

Imagine a fictional comparison desk. A merchant card records receipts, while a worker card lists time spent and payment owed. The first does not answer the second. To compare effects, ask what each person received, what costs they faced and how much choice they had. A modern collection object may help investigate design and exchange, but it is not a complete household budget. Nor did the end of the galleon connection in 1815 mean all Philippine trade stopped. Keep the network and its limits visible together.

fields.title: Prepare Your Galleon Evidence Report
fields.content:
Review five ideas. Manila and Acapulco were linked across the Pacific. Goods and silver moved through a wider network. Production places and loading ports were not always the same. People worked to make and move cargo. Departure and arrival were different stages, and valuable trade did not prove equal benefits for everyone.

Prepare a fictional exhibit report for another Grade 5 learner. Name the connection, identify a supporting clue and explain a limit. If you use the route diagram, call it a schematic rather than an exact sailing track. Keep workers visible alongside cargo, and compare peoples receipts, costs and choices before describing effects. Do not turn one journey into every voyage or treat 1815 as the end of all Philippine exchange.

The main quiz has five questions and three correct passes. If you need help, revisit the linked lesson before practice and a retry. This mission awards its configured reward once. It does not complete Chapter 9: Mission 5 and the chapter challenge are still being prepared.
